newsitem.title: UK: Insurers warned to gauge exposure to Year 2000 bug.
newsitem.headline: Insurers warned to gauge exposure to Year 2000 bug.

text.p: Insurance companies should check their portfolios to make sure they are not exposed to potentially catastrophic claims stemming from the year 2000 computer bug, a leading law firm warned on Wednesday.

Partners at solicitors Elborne Mitchell told an insurance seminar that huge costs will arise from fixing systems and from losses occurring if systems don't work when the clock ticks into the year 2000 in 941 days time.
And those facing the bills may well look for litigation targets with deep pockets to recover their losses, the firm said.
"No-one really knows if this will be an overhyped non-event or the biggest catastrophe ever to hit the insurance market," said partner Rosalind Jones.
"The only thing we can predict is that it will impact policies in ways we can't predict," she added.
"The only sensible advice we can give is to carry out an audit of policy exposure and act immediately," Jones said.

The year 2000 bug stems from a decision by programmers in the 1960's to save memory space by using the last two digits of a year instead of all four when referring to the date, a shorthand which continued in use until very recently .
When the year 2000 arrives and is read by the computer as '00', it either crashes the system or behaves as if the year were 1900. In either case the effect could be disastrous.
Partner Simon Brooks described a scenario where a supermarket failed to rectify the bug.

"In 1999 it starts rejecting goods with a sell-by date in the following year as 99 years out of date. When the year 2000 comes the system crashes meaning new supplies are not ordered, suppliers go unpaid, and credit control fails to collect amounts due," he said.
"It takes months and huge amounts of money to make the systems compliant, and the company makes huge losses and has to close a number of stores. Who do they look to for redress?" he said.
Brooks anticipated actions against information technology companies for giving poor advice or for selling non-compliant software.

Directors and officers could be sued for ignoring advice or for failing to recognise the problem and take action. And accountants could be sued for failing to spot the potential cost of compliance in the due diligence phase of acquisitions and mergers, Brooks said.

There is also potential for claims against product manufacturers and employers, stemming from injuries or damage caused by, for example, the failure of fire alarms and sprinklers, traffic lights, or automated refrigeration plants.

Claims are already beginning to come through, the law firm said, and insurers of computer errors and omissions cover, directors' and officers' cover, and professional indemnity cover can expect claims before 2000 as the cost of computer compliance work becomes known.
Jones listed policy exclusions or other defences that insurers might be able to use, but pointed out that even the cost of fighting these in court could be huge.
"We have seen a change in the attitude of courts to the way exclusions are put together. If there is any doubt, they will go in favour of the insured," she said.

"It is difficult to get an accurate definition of the problem to use in an exclusion. And it might not make commercial sense, as customers may go elsewhere their insurer tells them the year 2000 is not covered," said Brooks.
